label: When You Are Trapped by Addiction
framing: Scripture is honest about the chains we cannot break ourselves, naming the misery of doing the very thing we hate. It does not offer willpower as the cure but a freedom that comes from outside us, and it insists that the one in bondage is not beyond reach.
cultural: Paul wrote of the war within, willing the good but doing the evil, to a world that knew slavery as a literal condition and used it as the picture for sin's grip. His readers understood being owned by a master you could not escape on your own, which is exactly the language Scripture uses for the hold of sin on the body and will.
historical: The church has long known that some chains require more than resolve. The recovery movement of the twentieth century, rooted in Christian conviction through the Oxford Group, built the Twelve Steps on confession, surrender to a higher power, and honest community, recovering an ancient truth that no one is freed alone and that grace meets us at the bottom.
application: Tell the truth to at least one safe person today, because addiction lives in secrecy and dies in the light. Get real help, a counselor, a recovery group, a medical professional, or a treatment program, and understand that needing them is not weakness but wisdom. Expect setbacks without surrendering to them. If you or someone you love is in crisis, in the US call or text the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and for substance help call SAMHSA at 1-800-662-4357.

verses.text: I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh; for I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out. For I do not do the good I want to do. Instead, I keep on doing the evil I do not want to do.
verses.where: Paul describes wanting the good and not doing it, and doing the very thing he hates. Christians differ on whether he speaks of a believer's struggle or of life under the law without the Spirit. Either way, anyone caught in a habit they cannot break recognizes the voice, and the passage ends in thanks for rescue through Jesus Christ.

verses.text: “They struck me, but I feel no pain! They beat me, but I did not know it! When can I wake up to search for another drink?”
verses.where: A father paints a portrait of a man ruined by wine: woe, sorrow, quarrels, wounds without cause, and still, on waking, the first thought is the next drink. It is a strikingly exact picture of what we now call addiction. The pull it describes is old, and it is not unique to anyone.

verses.text: Jesus replied, “Truly, truly, I tell you, everyone who sins is a slave to sin. A slave is not a permanent member of the family, but a son belongs to it forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.
verses.where: Jesus tells people who believe they have never been slaves that everyone who sins is a slave to sin. A slave has no lasting place in the household, but a son does. Freedom here is not willpower; it is given by the Son, and he promises it is real.

verses.text: They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity. For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him.
verses.where: Peter describes false teachers who promise freedom while they are themselves enslaved. His summary line applies far beyond them: a person is a slave to whatever has mastered him. Anything can become a master, and the promise of freedom can come from the thing that is binding us.

verses.text: “Everything is permissible for me,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permissible for me,” but I will not be mastered by anything.
verses.where: Paul quotes a slogan from Corinth, everything is permissible for me, and answers it twice: not everything is beneficial, and I will not be mastered by anything. The question is not only whether a thing is allowed, but whether it is starting to own you.

verses.text: Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He saved them from their distress. He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death and broke away their chains.
verses.where: The psalm tells of prisoners sitting in darkness and chains, partly by their own rebellion, stumbling with no one to help. They cry to the LORD in their trouble, and he brings them out and breaks their chains. The psalm does not wait for them to deserve rescue before it comes.

verses.text: Finally he came to his senses and said, ‘How many of my father’s hired servants have plenty of food? But here I am, starving to death!
verses.where: The younger son has spent everything and is starving in a far country, feeding pigs. He comes to his senses and remembers his father's house. The turning point is honest awareness of where he is, and when he starts home, his father runs to meet him.

verses.text: Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey its desires. Do not present the parts of your body to sin as instruments of wickedness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life; and present the parts of your body to Him as instruments of righteousness. For sin shall not be your master, because you are not under law, but under grace.
verses.where: Paul pictures sin as a would-be king and the body's members as instruments that can be handed to one side or the other. He tells believers not to let sin reign, and gives the reason they can: sin shall not be your master, because you are under grace. The commands assume a real fight, and a real change of allegiance.

verses.text: Brothers, if someone is caught in a trespass, you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness. But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted. Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.
verses.where: Paul tells the church what to do when someone is caught in a sin: restore them gently, watch yourself, and carry one another's burdens. Recovery in the New Testament is never a private project. It is the whole community's work, done in humility.

verses.text: In every prayer for all of you, I always pray with joy, because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now, being confident of this, that He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.
verses.where: Paul writes from prison to a church he loves, confident that God, who began a good work in them, will carry it on to completion. The work is God's, and it is still in progress. Unfinished is not the same as failed.

links.label: Addiction and the Long Road Back

misread.taken: “The old has passed away” is sometimes used to say that a real Christian cannot still be struggling with an addiction, so that a relapse proves a person was never truly saved, or that needing treatment shows a lack of faith.
misread.says: Paul's sentence is short in Greek: if anyone in Christ, new creation. A person is made new, and belongs now to God's new world, which began when Christ rose. But the same Paul tells believers not to let sin reign in their bodies (Romans 6:12), and tells the church to restore gently anyone caught in a sin (Galatians 6:1); he assumes the new life is lived in a real fight. A relapse is not proof that grace failed. It is a reason to get more help, sooner.
misread.text: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!

whole: If you are in danger from what you are using, or have thoughts of hurting yourself, please get help today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line where you live, and in an emergency, your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Addiction rarely starts as a decision to be enslaved. It starts as relief: something that quiets pain, fills emptiness, steadies nerves, or simply feels good. Over time the relief costs more and gives less, and the person finds they cannot stop even when they want to. It may be alcohol, drugs, gambling, pornography, food, or a screen. Many people in its grip carry shame so heavy that they hide it from everyone, including God, and many Christians have been told, one way or another, that a real believer would simply stop.

The Bible knows the shape of this better than many of its readers. Proverbs describes a man who wakes up beaten and bruised and asks only for another drink. Paul describes wanting the good and doing what he hates. Jesus says that everyone who sins becomes a slave, and Peter says that a person is a slave to whatever masters him. Scripture names the moral reality without pretending it is simple. Addiction involves choices, and it also involves a bondage that choices alone do not break. That is why the Bible's answer is not merely try harder. It is rescue: the Son who sets free, the God who breaks chains for prisoners who cried out, and a church that carries burdens and restores gently.

So the wisdom here is to stop hiding and start being helped. Tell the truth to someone, as James urges, so that the secret loses its power. Get the help the body needs: a doctor, treatment, and where it fits, a recovery group. Put distance between yourself and what masters you, as Paul did with what he would not be mastered by. Expect a long road, with setbacks, and refuse to let a setback become a reason to give up. The younger son came to his senses in a pigsty and started home, rehearsing his speech. He was met before he arrived. God who began the work is not finished with it.

differ.share: Christians agree that addiction is real bondage, that people in its grip are responsible for seeking help and are not beyond grace, that freedom is God's gift, and that the church is called to walk with them.

views.name: Sin and false worship
views.body: Some Christians emphasize that addiction is at heart a disordered love, a way of looking to something other than God for what only God can give. They see repentance, grace and the church's close care as the center of recovery, with medical help for the body where it is needed.

views.name: Sickness as well as sin
views.body: Other Christians emphasize that addiction also changes the body and brain, so that it behaves like an illness that needs medical treatment. They see doctors, treatment programs and recovery groups as God's provision, alongside repentance and the church's care.

differ.after: Most Christians hold something of both, and both agree that shame and isolation make addiction worse, while honesty and help make freedom possible.

deep.sit: Who is one person who could know the whole truth about this, and what would it take to tell them this week?

prayer.lead: Psalm 142 was prayed in a cave by someone who felt trapped and alone. Pray its last lines for yourself: free my soul from prison.
prayer.text: Listen to my cry, for I am brought quite low. Rescue me from my pursuers, for they are too strong for me. Free my soul from prison, that I may praise Your name. The righteous will gather around me because of Your goodness to me.

careLines.text: If you are worn down by failing again and again, or caught in an addiction you cannot break, you are not alone, and you are not beyond help.
Please talk to someone: a doctor, a pastor, a counsellor, or a group that helps people with what you are facing.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country.
If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
